subject: research/energy-store-modelprice
professional: an energy-economics / power-systems researcher who reviews storage-valuation papers for Energy Economics or Applied Energy. They would check first that the price-taker charging rule is the optimum of its stated problem (cheapest hours under a charger-power limit), that the price model is truly out of sample, whether the storage-versus-heat-pump comparison prices both technologies against the same demand profile (timing and COP), and whether the result is placed against the forecast-error-in-storage-dispatch literature (Sioshansi, Denholm, Jenkin & Weiss 2009, Energy Economics 31(2), backcast dispatch captures most perfect-foresight arbitrage value; Walawalkar, Apt & Mancini 2007; for power-to-heat Bloess, Schill & Zerrahn 2018; for residual-load / merit-order price models Hirth 2013)

evidence.correctness: Every headline number reproduces and three parts of the pipeline recompute independently. Rerun of experiments/run.py (a copy that writes to the scratch dir, so the tree is untouched; /usr/bin/python3.13, 46 s) matches experiments/results.txt except one rounding digit: 2016 real weekly cheapest-quarter 0.0182 vs committed 0.0183 (the exact value is 0.01825, a half-way case that Python 3.12+'s compensated sum rounds down; every derived diff and verdict is unchanged). Independent scripts in the scratch dir energy/check.py, check2.py, check3.py (numpy 2.5 / scipy 1.18, reading the raw OPSD CSVs): (1) daily/weekly cheapest-quarter and Nov-Mar mean real prices 0.0216/0.0188, 0.0207/0.01825, 0.0230/0.0193, 0.0321/0.0276, 0.0265/0.0217 and hp 0.0319/0.0307/0.0388/0.0423/0.0391 equal section A; (2) a scipy HiGHS LP (buy 6 units in 24 h at <=1 unit/h) equals the cheapest-6 mean to 1e-17 on 10 real 2019 days, so the cheapest-quarter rule is the optimum of its window problem; (3) my own tie-averaged weighted PAVA isotonic fit, leave-one-year-out, gives resid means 0.0375/0.0397/0.0362/0.0328/0.0317 (README 0.036-0.040 over-, 2018-19 under-), house weekly diffs +0.0080/+0.0098/+0.0044/-0.0032/-0.0097 (section H), and agreement 32/37/21 of 40 for resid/resid+/merit (section C); (4) break-even by bisection 0.0375/0.0372/0.0386/0.0392/0.0387 equals section F. The cost model itself (energy-thermal-cost) was used as given, not re-derived.
evidence.completeness: All four claimed analyses exist and run end to end: verdict agreement (sections B, C, G), weekly failure and oracle (H, G), break-even (F), executed charging (D, E); figure.py parses results.txt into weekly.svg; 6 tests pass; live page https://marisstella.app/research/energy-store-modelprice/ returns 200 and carries the 32-of-40 headline. Next steps (fuel/carbon regressor, cost CI, true forecast) are listed as open, not claimed.
evidence.verification: `cd research/energy-store-modelprice && python3.13 -m pytest tests -q`: 6 passed in 1.35 s. Four mutations of model.py via quality_mutate.py: paying the planned instead of the actual price (line 41) and reversing the charge-hour sort (line 40) are caught; training on all five years instead of leave-one-year-out (line 24, the property the whole study rests on) survives, and changing the tie band from <= to < (line 56) survives. No test pins any headline number (32/40, 21/40, weekly 0/5) or the leave-one-out split.
evidence.craft: Read model.py (57 lines), run.py (107), figure.py (28), test_model.py (40). Small, readable, stdlib only, reuses the sibling packages instead of copying them. Defects: run.py recomputes every diff three times (sections B, D, G, H call diff() again), which is why it takes 46 s here; it writes results.txt itself and the README also tells the reader to redirect stdout into the same file; verdict(d, 0.0) is called with a pre-subtracted diff, an awkward API; sys.path manipulation at import time in model.py.
evidence.claims: Checked 11 README/project.json claims against results.txt and my recomputation: 32/40 vs 21/40, 30 of 30 non-weekly cells, weekly 0/5 house and 2/5 district, oracle restores 4/5, mean-level over/understatement ranges, break-even 0.038-0.039 vs 0.037-0.039, cheap-quarter offsets, executed gaps 0.0004-0.0011 and 0.0006-0.0010, merit gaps +0.0041/+0.0143, merit range 0.003-0.020 (project.json) all backed. One wrong: README line 15 says the pump wins the house weekly case 'in two [years] in the real series'; section B/H show one pump win (2018) and one tie (2019, -0.0005). Runtime 'about 20 s' was 46 s here (machine-dependent). Limitations are unusually candid (correlated cells, no significance test, tie band is a choice, LOYO sees later years, wholesale only). Disclaimer of AI assistance present.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could rerun and extend it in minutes (stdlib, deterministic, data committed). The question (does a technology verdict survive a modelled price) is a sensible one, and the scheduling result (model-ranked charging costs 0.0007-0.0009 EUR/kWh over perfect foresight) agrees with Sioshansi et al. 2009's finding that backcast/forecast dispatch captures most arbitrage value, but no prior work is cited, so the reader cannot tell what is new. The 32/40 headline mixes 20 monthly/seasonal cells that every price source including the flat price gets right; on the 20 informative daily+weekly cells it is 12/20 vs 1/20 (the README does say all misses are weekly). The 'fails in sign' weekly finding is about a margin the README itself says is inside cost uncertainty. Tie-band sensitivity (my check3.py): resid 34/32/32/30/29 and merit 22/22/21/21/21 of 40 at tol 0/0.001/0.002/0.003/0.005, so the ranking is robust to the one free parameter.
evidence.domain: The price-taker charging rule is correct for its stated problem (LP check). The isotonic residual-load price curve is a defensible merit-order proxy. Departures a reviewer would raise first: (a) the store is priced on the cheapest quarter of all 365 daily (or 52 weekly) windows, delivering heat year-round, while the heat pump pays the Nov-Mar mean, so the two technologies serve different demand profiles; restricting the store to heating-season days gives 0.0199/0.0200/0.0238/0.0285/0.0262 against 0.0216/0.0207/0.0230/0.0321/0.0265 (shifts of -0.004 to +0.001), comparable to the whole weekly margin; (b) the air-source heat pump has a constant COP (energy-thermal-cost cost.py:60), ignoring that COP falls in cold hours that coincide with high prices, which biases against the store and is not mentioned in this README; (c) no levies/grid fees (stated). Both (a) and (b) are inherited from energy-thermal-real, but they bear directly on the weekly verdict this project studies.

defects.what: The leave-one-year-out split, the property that makes 'resid' a model rather than a fit, is untested: training on all five years (including the held-out one) leaves all 6 tests green.

Store and heat pump serve different demand profiles: the store buys the cheapest quarter of all 365 daily / 52 weekly windows (heat delivered year-round) while the pump pays the Nov-Mar mean, and the air-source COP is constant. Heating-season-only store prices shift by -0.004 to +0.001 EUR/kWh, the size of the whole weekly margin the project studies. Inherited from energy-thermal-real and not stated in this README's limitations.

No prior work cited: the forecast-error-in-storage-dispatch literature (Sioshansi et al. 2009; Walawalkar et al. 2007) already finds model/backcast-scheduled storage captures most perfect-foresight value, so the 'scheduling costs little' result is a confirmation, not new; the 32/40 headline also counts 20 monthly/seasonal cells every source gets right (informative cells 12/20 vs 1/20).
README says the pump wins the house weekly case in two real years; results show one pump win (2018) and one tie (2019).
Tie-band boundary (<= vs <) and every headline count (32/40, 21/40, weekly 0/5) are unpinned by tests.
Runtime 'about 20 s' was 46 s (run.py recomputes each diff in three sections); results.txt line 8 2016 weekly 0.0183 reruns as 0.0182 on Python 3.13 (exact value 0.01825, half-way rounding).

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible study. Every headline number reproduces on rerun and independently: my own PAVA leave-one-year-out fit gives the same 32/37/21 of 40 agreement and weekly diffs, an LP confirms the cheapest-quarter charging rule is optimal for its window problem, and bisection matches the break-even prices. Limitations are candid. It does not meet the bar on verification (2): the leave-one-year-out split, the property the whole study rests on, can be removed without a test failing, and the tie band is unpinned. Fitness and domain are 2: no prior work is cited (Sioshansi et al. 2009 already shows model-scheduled storage captures most perfect-foresight value), and the store-versus-pump comparison prices the store on year-round cheapest hours against a heating-season pump with constant COP, a mismatch of the same size as the weekly margin under study. One small wrong count: README line 15 'against two in the real series' should be one (plus a tie). Finished: yes; meets the bar: no.
